title: Self-Certifying Transport MCMC via Dual Spectral-Gap Certificates

paper.title: Self-Certifying Transport MCMC via Dual Spectral-Gap Certificates
paper.abstract:
Abstract We propose CerT-MCMC, a framework that equips learned-transport Markov chain Monte Carlo with automatic, rigorous convergence certificates.
A normalising flow maps a Gaussian reference to an approximation of the target posterior; the same flow then serves as both the independence Metropolis–Hastings proposal and the basis for a computable spectral-gap bound.
We develop two complementary certificates.
The covering certificate bounds the weight-ratio oscillation over the full proposal support via finite-sample covering arguments, yielding full-support spectral-gap bounds when a conservative gradient bound is available; its correction term scales as O ( n − 1 / D ) O(n^{-1/D}) , making it rapidly weak and eventually vacuous as dimension increases.
The quantile-core certificate restricts attention to a high-probability residual core on which the oscillation is controlled by one-dimensional empirical quantiles, with a finite-sample probability slack of O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) , independent of the ambient dimension.
On synthetic targets ( D = 2 D=2 – 20 20 ), structural-engineering posteriors ( D = 6 , 8 D=6,8 ), real-data logistic regression on the Heart Disease data set ( D = 13 D=13 ), and synthetic Bayesian logistic regression ( D = 20 D=20 ), the quantile-core certificate delivers non-vacuous spectral-gap bounds where the covering certificate is vacuous, and its spectral-gap proxy tracks empirical effective sample sizes within 7 % 7\% .
A negative control experiment confirms that the certificate discriminates flow quality by a factor exceeding 10 × 10\times , whereas acceptance rates differ by only 1.15 × 1.15\times .
To our knowledge, the dual-certificate framework is the first to provide automatic, dimension-aware convergence certificates for learned-transport MCMC, distinguishing genuine transport failure from proof-technique limitations.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the workhorse of Bayesian computation, yet verifying that a chain has converged remains an open problem. Practitioners rely on heuristic diagnostics—trace plots, the R ^ \hat{R} statistic ( Gelman & Rubin 1992 , Brooks & Gelman 1998 , Vehtari et al. 2021 ) , effective sample size estimates ( Vats et al. 2019 ) —that can detect certain pathologies but cannot certify convergence. A spectral-gap bound, by contrast, provides a certificate : a computable quantity that guarantees the chain mixes within a known number of iterations. Such certificates exist in theory ( Mengersen & Tweedie 1996 , Rosenthal 1995 , Tierney 1994 ) but have rarely been turned into practical tools, because they require tight control of quantities—such as the importance-weight oscillation—that depend on the unknown target distribution. As Bayesian workflows increasingly rely on learned, adaptive, and amortised proposals, convergence assessment becomes not easier but harder: the transition kernel itself is partly learned and high-dimensional, making auditability a central requirement for modern Bayesian computation. A recent line of work has shown that normalising flows ( Rezende & Mohamed 2015 , Dinh et al. 2017 , Papamakarios et al. 2021 ) can serve as powerful MCMC proposals. By training an invertible neural network T ϕ T_{\phi} to map a simple reference distribution (typically a Gaussian) to an approximation of the target, one obtains an adaptive, amortised proposal for independence Metropolis–Hastings (IMH). Existing methods focus on using this proposal to improve empirical mixing: Parno & Marzouk (2018) use transport maps to accelerate MCMC in moderate dimensions; Hoffman et al. (2019) apply normalising flows to precondition Hamiltonian Monte Carlo; Gabrié et al. (2022) and Wong et al. (2023) develop adaptive flow-based samplers that demonstrate strong empirical efficiency. All of these methods preserve the correct stationary distribution via the Metropolis–Hastings accept/reject step, but none provides a computable convergence guarantee. The central question of this paper is different from that of the transport-MCMC literature: Prior work asks: can a learned proposal improve mixing? We ask: can a learned proposal certify its own convergence? We show that the answer is yes in two restricted but operationally useful senses, each confronting the fundamental tension between the dimensionality of the parameter space and the finite-sample cost of certification.

sections.text: When the proposal q ϕ q_{\phi} is used in an IMH kernel targeting π \pi , the acceptance probability depends on the importance-weight ratio w ⁡ ( z ) = π z ​ ( z ) / q 0 ​ ( z ) w(z)=\pi_{z}(z)/q_{0}(z) , where π z \pi_{z} is the pullback of π \pi to the latent z z -space. The Mengersen–Tweedie theorem ( Mengersen & Tweedie 1996 ) states that the spectral gap of the IMH kernel is at least 2 / ( 1 + e C ) 2/(1+e^{C}) , where C = osc ⁡ ( log ⁡ w ) C=\mathrm{osc}(\log w) is the oscillation of the log-weight over the proposal support. If T ϕ T_{\phi} is a perfect transport map, log ⁡ w \log w is constant and C = 0 C=0 ; for an imperfect flow, C C measures the quality of the learned transport. Crucially, the residual r ⁡ ( z ) = log ⁡ w ⁡ ( z ) r(z)=\log w(z) is computable for any z z given T ϕ T_{\phi} and π \pi , without knowing the normalising constant of π \pi . This opens a path to data-driven certification: draw samples from the proposal, evaluate r r at each sample, and bound the oscillation from the observed values.

sections.heading: Certificate I: covering the full support.
sections.text: The most direct approach bounds osc ⁡ ( r ) \mathrm{osc}(r) by the sample range plus a Lipschitz correction for the gap between sample points. Given n n certification samples in D D dimensions, the worst-case gap scales as ε ∗ ∼ n − 1 / D \varepsilon^{*}\sim n^{-1/D} —the classical curse of dimensionality for covering arguments. For D = 2 D=2 or 5 5 , this yields non-vacuous certificates at practical sample sizes; for D ≳ 6 D\gtrsim 6 , the correction dominates and the certificate rapidly weakens; by D = 20 D=20 it is effectively vacuous. We call this the covering certificate (Certificate I) and develop it formally in Section 2.3 .

sections.heading: Certificate II: the quantile-core certificate.
sections.text: The covering certificate’s failure in moderate dimensions is not a failure of the sampler. Empirically, a well-trained flow produces a residual r ⁡ ( z ) r(z) that is highly concentrated: at D = 10 D=10 , the central 99 % 99\% interquantile range is only 11 % 11\% of the full range (Table 1 ). Certificate I pays an exponentially growing price to control the remaining 1 % 1\% of boundary outliers. Certificate II avoids this entirely by restricting attention to a data-defined residual core —the set of z z -values whose residuals fall within the central quantile range—and certifying the IMH kernel restricted to this core. The key insight is that the certified oscillation on the core depends only on one-dimensional quantile estimation, whose finite-sample probability slack is O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) via the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality, independent of the ambient dimension D D . Moreover, the normalising constants in the restricted importance weight cancel exactly (Section 3 ), so the Mengersen–Tweedie theorem applies directly to the core-restricted kernel. The result is a computable, high-confidence spectral-gap lower bound that remains non-vacuous through D = 20 D=20 on the banana target and on real structural-engineering posteriors where Certificate I is completely vacuous. In effect, CerT-MCMC changes the role of learned transport from a black-box accelerator into an auditable object of Bayesian computation: the same map that proposes moves also exposes residual geometry from which finite-sample convergence certificates can be constructed.

sections.heading: Dual-certificate framework.
sections.text: Certificates I and II are complementary. Certificate I provides a full-support worst-case guarantee wherever the covering argument is tractable. Certificate II provides a high-mass core guarantee in all dimensions, honestly reporting the uncertified tail fraction 2 ​ ρ 2\rho . Together they yield a four-level diagnostic taxonomy (Figure 1 d): full certificate success (both certificates non-vacuous), core certificate success (Certificate II non-vacuous, Certificate I vacuous—the flow is good but the covering proof is the bottleneck), transport degradation (Certificate II non-vacuous but weak, reflecting genuine flow quality decline), and transport failure (Certificate II vacuous, indicating a poor flow). This taxonomy distinguishes proof-technique limitations from genuine transport failure—a distinction that standard convergence diagnostics do not directly provide.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (i) We propose CerT-MCMC, a framework that equips learned-transport MCMC with automatic, rigorous spectral-gap certificates derived from the same normalising flow used as the IMH proposal. (ii) We develop the covering certificate (Certificate I), prove a worst-case Ω ( n − 1 / D ) \Omega(n^{-1/D}) lower bound for pointwise full-support Lipschitz certification (Proposition 2 ), and thereby formalise the covering barrier that motivates Certificate II. (iii) We develop the quantile-core certificate (Certificate II), which bounds the core oscillation via empirical quantiles with a finite-sample probability slack of O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) independent of D D , and prove a spectral-gap theorem for the core-restricted IMH kernel. (iv) We demonstrate empirically that the spectral-gap proxy from Certificate II tracks actual mixing efficiency: on Bayesian logistic regression ( D = 20 D=20 ), the proxy at a fixed trimming level matches the observed effective sample size within 7 % 7\% . (v) We provide a comprehensive experimental evaluation on synthetic targets ( D = 2 D=2 – 20 20 ), structural-engineering posteriors ( D = 6 , 8 D=6,8 ), and Bayesian logistic regression ( D = 20 D=20 ), showing that Certificate II delivers non-vacuous guarantees wherever Certificate I is vacuous and correctly identifies transport quality differences across targets.

sections.heading: Organisation.
sections.text: Section 2 introduces the transport-map framework, the Mengersen–Tweedie bound, and Certificate I. Section 3 develops the quantile-core certificate (Certificate II) with full proofs. Section 4 relates the core certificate to mixing efficiency. Section 5 presents experiments. Section 6 discusses limitations and future directions.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: This paper introduces CerT-MCMC, a framework for equipping learned-transport MCMC with rigorous, computable convergence certificates. Two complementary certificates—the covering certificate (Certificate I) and the quantile-core certificate (Certificate II)—provide a multi-resolution view of sampler quality. We discuss the implications, limitations, and directions for future work.

sections.heading: Auditable Bayesian computation.
sections.text: Modern Bayesian workflows increasingly rely on learned components—normalising flows, neural network surrogates, adaptive proposals—that improve empirical performance but resist classical convergence analysis. The dual-certificate framework offers a step toward auditable learned Bayesian computation: the same normalising flow that serves as the proposal also produces a certificate quantifying how well it has learned the target. Certificate I provides a full-support worst-case guarantee when the covering argument is tractable; Certificate II provides a scalable, mass-aware alternative that remains informative in dimensions where Certificate I is vacuous. Together they separate proof-technique limitations from genuine transport failure—a distinction that standard convergence diagnostics do not directly provide.

sections.heading: Diagnostic taxonomy.
sections.text: The dual-certificate framework induces a four-level diagnostic (Figure 1 d): (i) full certificate success , where both certificates are non-vacuous (banana D = 2 , 5 D=2,5 ); (ii) core certificate success with covering gap , where Certificate II is non-vacuous but Certificate I is vacuous, indicating that the flow has learned the target well but the covering proof is the bottleneck (banana D = 6 D=6 – 10 10 , sailboat, shear building); (iii) transport degradation , where Certificate II remains non-vacuous but with a weaker gap ( γ < 0.5 \gamma<0.5 ), reflecting genuine flow capacity limitations (banana D = 20 D=20 , logistic regression D = 20 D=20 ); and (iv) transport failure , where Certificate II is vacuous, indicating that the flow does not approximate the target adequately (negative control, Section 5.6 ). Notably, the negative control experiment shows that Certificate II discriminates flow quality by a factor of 10 10 – 13 × 13\times at ρ = 0.01 \rho=0.01 , whereas acceptance rates differ by only 1.15 × 1.15\times .

sections.heading: Certificate I’s systematic false negatives.
sections.text: A finding with methodological implications is that Certificate I systematically misclassifies well-functioning samplers as uncertifiable in moderate dimensions. The shear building ( D = 8 D=8 ), which Certificate I renders vacuous ( C I > 16 C_{\mathrm{I}}>16 ), achieves a core spectral gap of γ II = 0.43 \gamma_{\mathrm{II}}=0.43 at ρ = 0.01 \rho=0.01 —better than the sailboat ( D = 6 D=6 , γ II = 0.36 \gamma_{\mathrm{II}}=0.36 ). Certificate I’s failure is driven not by transport quality but by rare boundary outliers: the central 99 % 99\% of the residual accounts for only 3 3 – 11 % 11\% of the full oscillation (Table 1 ). This suggests that worst-case covering certificates, while rigorous, may substantially underestimate the quality of learned transport in practice.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: Several limitations should be noted. First, Certificate II certifies the IMH kernel restricted to the data-defined residual core G ~ ρ \tilde{G}_{\rho} , not the full K α K_{\alpha} -restricted chain. The core captures at least ( 1 − 2 ​ ρ ) (1-2\rho) of the proposal mass, and empirically a comparable fraction of the target mass in the well-matched cases studied (Table 8 ), but a rigorous target-mass conversion—e.g., via self-normalised importance sampling concentration inequalities—is left to future work. Second, the framework is specific to independence Metropolis–Hastings. Extension to other kernels with explicit weight ratios (preconditioned Crank–Nicolson, sequential Monte Carlo) is conceptually straightforward—the quantile-core construction applies to any setting where the acceptance weight is computable—but requires kernel-specific spectral-gap theory. Third, the spectral-gap ESS proxy (Section 4 ) is a conservative lower-bound-scale estimate, not a point prediction of mixing time; its practical value lies in tracking relative mixing efficiency across targets and flow conditions rather than in producing exact ESS numbers.

sections.heading: Real-data stress test: the role of preconditioning.
sections.text: As a practical stress test, we applied CerT-MCMC to Bayesian logistic regression on the Wisconsin Breast Cancer data set ( D = 30 D=30 , n = 569 n=569 ; Street et al. 1993 ). Without posterior preconditioning, the RealNVP proposal failed to approximate the posterior geometry: the IMH acceptance rate was 0.05 % 0.05\% and std ⁡ ( r ) = 4.3 \mathrm{std}(r)=4.3 . Laplace whitening—reparametrising via the Hessian at the posterior mode—substantially improved the proposal, increasing acceptance to approximately 34 % 34\% and reducing std ⁡ ( r ) \mathrm{std}(r) to 1.4 1.4 . However, the quantile-core certificate remained modest ( γ II ≈ 0.026 \gamma_{\mathrm{II}}\approx 0.026 at ρ = 0.05 \rho=0.05 ; see the Supplementary Material (Section D)). This stress test illustrates two practical points. First, standard statistical preconditioning is often necessary before applying flow-based proposals to correlated real-data posteriors. Second, CerT-MCMC honestly reports when the learned transport is insufficient—a property that distinguishes it from heuristic diagnostics. More expressive flow architectures or posterior-adapted reference distributions may be needed for D ≥ 30 D\geq 30 real-data targets; we leave this to future work.

sections.heading: Future directions.
sections.text: Several extensions are natural. Certificate-aware training: The CerT-OG-Anneal objective minimises the full oscillation osc ⁡ ( r ) \mathrm{osc}(r) ; a more targeted objective could directly minimise Var μ K ​ ( r ) \mathrm{Var}_{\mu_{K}}(r) or the quantile range, better aligning training with Certificate II. Target-mass certification: A rigorous finite-sample bound on π z ​ ( G ~ ρ ) \pi_{z}(\tilde{G}_{\rho}) using concentration inequalities for self-normalised sums would complete the theoretical picture. sections.heading: Appendix A Covering Barrier: Experimental Confirmation
sections.text: The covering certificate’s n − 1 / D n^{-1/D} correction term raises a natural question: can a more careful covering argument recover a faster rate? We investigated three refinements of Certificate I, none of which breaks the n − 1 / D n^{-1/D} barrier. The first, local Lipschitz partitioning , subdivides K α K_{\alpha} into cells and replaces the global gradient bound ‖ ∇ r ‖ sup \|\nabla r\|_{\sup} with cell-wise local bounds. While the local Lipschitz constants do shrink on a finer partition, the number of cells required to cover K α K_{\alpha} grows faster than the constants decrease, so the product governing the correction term increases rather than decreases. The covering cost growth thus dominates any gain from sharper local gradients. The second refinement, pointwise gradient correction , replaces the worst-case gradient bound with empirically estimated gradients at each sample point. This tightens the constant prefactor but leaves the n − 1 / D n^{-1/D} scaling in ε ∗ \varepsilon^{*} untouched, since the inter-sample gap is a geometric property of the design and independent of the gradient estimate. The third, boundary truncation , shrinks the certification region to exclude low-mass boundary shells. Truncation improves the absolute correction by roughly 8 × 8\times at D = 6 D=6 , but the improvement is a constant factor: the exponent of the n − 1 / D n^{-1/D} scaling is unchanged, so the barrier reappears at slightly higher dimension. Together these experiments confirm that the n − 1 / D n^{-1/D} rate is intrinsic to the covering approach and motivate the quantile-core construction of Certificate II, which sidesteps covering entirely. Full numerical results are reported in the supplementary experiments.

sections.text: We use the UCI Heart Disease Statlog subset ( n = 270 n=270 , D = 13 D=13 ), obtained via OpenML. A normalising flow maps a Gaussian reference to an approximation of the target posterior; the same flow then serves as both the independence Metropolis–Hastings proposal and the basis for a computable spectral-gap bound. We develop two complementary certificates. The covering certificate bounds the weight-ratio oscillation over the full proposal support via finite-sample covering arguments, yielding full-support spectral-gap bounds when a conservative gradient bound is available; its correction term scales as O ( n − 1 / D ) O(n^{-1/D}) , making it rapidly weak and eventually vacuous as dimension increases. The quantile-core certificate restricts attention to a high-probability residual core on which the oscillation is controlled by one-dimensional empirical quantiles, with a finite-sample probability slack of O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) , independent of the ambient dimension. On synthetic targets ( D = 2 D=2 – 20 20 ), structural-engineering posteriors ( D = 6 , 8 D=6,8 ), real-data logistic regression on the Heart Disease data set ( D = 13 D=13 ), and synthetic Bayesian logistic regression ( D = 20 D=20 ), the quantile-core certificate delivers non-vacuous spectral-gap bounds where the covering certificate is vacuous, and its spectral-gap proxy tracks empirical effective sample sizes within 7 % 7\% . A negative control experiment confirms that the certificate discriminates flow quality by a factor exceeding 10 × 10	imes , whereas acceptance rates differ by only 1.15 × 1.15	imes . To our knowledge, the dual-certificate framework is the first to provide automatic, dimension-aware convergence certificates for learned-transport MCMC, distinguishing genuine transport failure from proof-technique limitations. Keywords: Markov chain Monte Carlo; normalising flows; spectral gap; convergence certificate; independence Metropolis–Hastings; Bayesian computation. 1 Introduction Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) is the workhorse of Bayesian computation, yet verifying that a chain has converged remains an open problem. Practitioners rely on heuristic diagnostics—trace plots, the R ^ \hat{R} statistic ( Gelman & Rubin 1992 , Brooks & Gelman 1998 , Vehtari et al. 2021 ) , effective sample size estimates ( Vats et al. 2019 ) —that can detect certain pathologies but cannot certify convergence. A spectral-gap bound, by contrast, provides a certificate : a computable quantity that guarantees the chain mixes within a known number of iterations. Such certificates exist in theory ( Mengersen & Tweedie 1996 , Rosenthal 1995 , Tierney 1994 ) but have rarely been turned into practical tools, because they require tight control of quantities—such as the importance-weight oscillation—that depend on the unknown target distribution. As Bayesian workflows increasingly rely on learned, adaptive, and amortised proposals, convergence assessment becomes not easier but harder: the transition kernel itself is partly learned and high-dimensional, making auditability a central requirement for modern Bayesian computation. A recent line of work has shown that normalising flows ( Rezende & Mohamed 2015 , Dinh et al. 2017 , Papamakarios et al. 2021 ) can serve as powerful MCMC proposals. By training an invertible neural network T ϕ T_{\phi} to map a simple reference distribution (typically a Gaussian) to an approximation of the target, one obtains an adaptive, amortised proposal for independence Metropolis–Hastings (IMH). Existing methods focus on using this proposal to improve empirical mixing: Parno & Marzouk (2018) use transport maps to accelerate MCMC in moderate dimensions; Hoffman et al. (2019) apply normalising flows to precondition Hamiltonian Monte Carlo; Gabrié et al. (2022) and Wong et al. (2023) develop adaptive flow-based samplers that demonstrate strong empirical efficiency. All of these methods preserve the correct stationary distribution via the Metropolis–Hastings accept/reject step, but none provides a computable convergence guarantee. The central question of this paper is different from that of the transport-MCMC literature: Prior work asks: can a learned proposal improve mixing? We ask: can a learned proposal certify its own convergence? We show that the answer is yes in two restricted but operationally useful senses, each confronting the fundamental tension between the dimensionality of the parameter space and the finite-sample cost of certification. The certification route. When the proposal q ϕ q_{\phi} is used in an IMH kernel targeting π \pi , the acceptance probability depends on the importance-weight ratio w ⁡ ( z ) = π z ​ ( z ) / q 0 ​ ( z ) w(z)=\pi_{z}(z)/q_{0}(z) , where π z \pi_{z} is the pullback of π \pi to the latent z z -space. The Mengersen–Tweedie theorem ( Mengersen & Tweedie 1996 ) states that the spectral gap of the IMH kernel is at least 2 / ( 1 + e C ) 2/(1+e^{C}) , where C = osc ⁡ ( log ⁡ w ) C=\mathrm{osc}(\log w) is the oscillation of the log-weight over the proposal support. If T ϕ T_{\phi} is a perfect transport map, log ⁡ w \log w is constant and C = 0 C=0 ; for an imperfect flow, C C measures the quality of the learned transport. Crucially, the residual r ⁡ ( z ) = log ⁡ w ⁡ ( z ) r(z)=\log w(z) is computable for any z z given T ϕ T_{\phi} and π \pi , without knowing the normalising constant of π \pi . This opens a path to data-driven certification: draw samples from the proposal, evaluate r r at each sample, and bound the oscillation from the observed values. Certificate I: covering the full support. The most direct approach bounds osc ⁡ ( r ) \mathrm{osc}(r) by the sample range plus a Lipschitz correction for the gap between sample points. Given n n certification samples in D D dimensions, the worst-case gap scales as ε ∗ ∼ n − 1 / D \varepsilon^{*}\sim n^{-1/D} —the classical curse of dimensionality for covering arguments. For D = 2 D=2 or 5 5 , this yields non-vacuous certificates at practical sample sizes; for D ≳ 6 D\gtrsim 6 , the correction dominates and the certificate rapidly weakens; by D = 20 D=20 it is effectively vacuous. We call this the covering certificate (Certificate I) and develop it formally in Section 2.3 . Certificate II: the quantile-core certificate. The covering certificate’s failure in moderate dimensions is not a failure of the sampler. Empirically, a well-trained flow produces a residual r ⁡ ( z ) r(z) that is highly concentrated: at D = 10 D=10 , the central 99 % 99\% interquantile range is only 11 % 11\% of the full range (Table 1 ). Certificate I pays an exponentially growing price to control the remaining 1 % 1\% of boundary outliers. Certificate II avoids this entirely by restricting attention to a data-defined residual core —the set of z z -values whose residuals fall within the central quantile range—and certifying the IMH kernel restricted to this core. The key insight is that the certified oscillation on the core depends only on one-dimensional quantile estimation, whose finite-sample probability slack is O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) via the Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz inequality, independent of the ambient dimension D D . Moreover, the normalising constants in the restricted importance weight cancel exactly (Section 3 ), so the Mengersen–Tweedie theorem applies directly to the core-restricted kernel. The result is a computable, high-confidence spectral-gap lower bound that remains non-vacuous through D = 20 D=20 on the banana target and on real structural-engineering posteriors where Certificate I is completely vacuous. In effect, CerT-MCMC changes the role of learned transport from a black-box accelerator into an auditable object of Bayesian computation: the same map that proposes moves also exposes residual geometry from which finite-sample convergence certificates can be constructed. Dual-certificate framework. Certificates I and II are complementary. Certificate I provides a full-support worst-case guarantee wherever the covering argument is tractable. Certificate II provides a high-mass core guarantee in all dimensions, honestly reporting the uncertified tail fraction 2 ​ ρ 2ho . Together they yield a four-level diagnostic taxonomy (Figure 1 d): full certificate success (both certificates non-vacuous), core certificate success (Certificate II non-vacuous, Certificate I vacuous—the flow is good but the covering proof is the bottleneck), transport degradation (Certificate II non-vacuous but weak, reflecting genuine flow quality decline), and transport failure (Certificate II vacuous, indicating a poor flow). This taxonomy distinguishes proof-technique limitations from genuine transport failure—a distinction that standard convergence diagnostics do not directly provide. Contributions. (i) We propose CerT-MCMC, a framework that equips learned-transport MCMC with automatic, rigorous spectral-gap certificates derived from the same normalising flow used as the IMH proposal. (ii) We develop the covering certificate (Certificate I), prove a worst-case Ω ( n − 1 / D ) \Omega(n^{-1/D}) lower bound for pointwise full-support Lipschitz certification (Proposition 2 ), and thereby formalise the covering barrier that motivates Certificate II. (iii) We develop the quantile-core certificate (Certificate II), which bounds the core oscillation via empirical quantiles with a finite-sample probability slack of O ( n − 1 / 2 ) O(n^{-1/2}) independent of D D , and prove a spectral-gap theorem for the core-restricted IMH kernel.
